messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 56
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Musician
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 71

# Clinical Vignette: Martin

Martin is a 56-year-old married man who has spent the better part of his adult life as a professional musician — a session guitarist whose work has carried him through recording studios and small concert venues across Europe. He describes music as the language he has always trusted most, the one place where he has felt genuinely at home in his own skin. That sense of home began to collapse three years ago, and he is still, as he puts it, "trying to find the door back in."

The assault occurred at an industry event in a city he had traveled to for a recording session. A colleague — someone he had known professionally for over a decade, someone he considered a friend — sexually assaulted him in a hotel room after an evening of drinks. Martin had not anticipated it. He had not, in his own words, even had a framework for it. He is a large man, physically strong, and the assault left him with a confusion that ran deeper than the act itself: a corrosive, grinding shame that he could not explain to himself and therefore could not begin to explain to anyone else. He drove home the next morning, told his wife he was tired, and said nothing more for nearly two years.

In those first months, Martin continued to work because stopping felt more dangerous than continuing. He took studio bookings, showed up, played. But something had shifted in the architecture of how he moved through the world. He began avoiding any social context connected to the industry — declining session invitations, canceling appearances, withdrawing from the loose community of musicians he had cultivated over decades. He told himself he was simply getting older, that the late nights no longer suited him. He did not tell himself the truth.

At home, his wife noticed that he had become unreachable in some essential way. He was present in the house but absent from her. He slept poorly, lying rigid in the dark for hours, and when sleep did come it brought with it a recurring dream in which he is back in that hotel corridor, walking toward a door he already knows he should not open. He wakes from it with his heart hammering, drenched, needing several minutes to locate himself in the present. During the day, intrusive images arrive without warning — triggered by something as incidental as a particular cologne, a certain quality of light in a room, the sound of a deadbolt turning. When these moments come, his body responds as though the assault is happening again: his chest tightens, his hands go cold, and he feels a wave of nausea that he has learned to manage by going very still and very quiet until it passes.

He has largely stopped playing guitar for pleasure. He still fulfills professional obligations, but the private relationship he once had with the instrument — the late evenings noodling through ideas, the sense of discovery — has dried up. He cannot fully account for why. He says only that when he sits down to play for himself, something feels wrong, as though he is performing for an audience he cannot see and cannot trust.

Martin eventually told his wife what had happened after she found him sitting alone in the kitchen at three in the morning, crying without knowing he was crying. Her response was one of steadiness and grief, and he is grateful for it, though he finds intimacy between them difficult now in ways that pain him and that he does not know how to repair. He carries a pervasive sense that he is fundamentally altered — that the man who walked into that hotel room no longer exists, and that the one who walked out has been pretending ever since.

He presents now as guarded but earnest, choosing his words with the same deliberate care he brings to a difficult chord passage — as though precision might protect him, or at least honor the weight of what he is trying to say.
